Response curve for a channel

Source: R/contributions.R
response_curve.Rd

Predicted response across a range of adstocked spend, derived from the fitted saturation parameters. spend_for() is the inverse: the adstocked spend that achieves a target response.

Usage

response_curve(spend, coefficient, type = "hill", ...)

spend_for(target, coefficient, type = "hill", max_spend = NULL, ...)

Arguments

spend

Numeric vector of adstocked spend levels to evaluate, in the units the saturation curve was fitted on (see Details), finite and non-negative. response_curve() only; spend_for() has no such argument.

coefficient

The channel's fitted coefficient.

type

Saturation curve type, as in saturate(), or "none" for a linear response.

...

Passed to saturate(), for example half_max and shape.

target

Target response level. spend_for() only. It must lie on the side of the response at zero spend that spending moves towards: above it for a positive coefficient, below it for a negative one.

max_spend

Upper bound of the search interval for spend_for(). Defaults to 1000 times the curve's spend-scaled parameter (half_max, km, or log(2)/rate). saturate_power() and "none" have no such parameter, so max_spend is required there.

Value

response_curve() returns a data frame with columns spend (the levels given), response (the coefficient times the curve at each level) and marginal (the slope of response there, as mroi() computes it), one row per element of spend and in the same order. It has class mm_response_curve, with a plot() method. spend_for() returns a single adstocked spend level, or NA_real_ with a warning when the target is not reachable within max_spend. A target that no amount of spend can reach, such as a negative response from a channel with a positive coefficient, is an error.

Details

spend is the saturation curve's input. When the regressor came from media_transform(), that is adstocked spend: the media pressure in a period, carryover included, rather than the spend of that period alone. Under a normalised kernel, the default, a steady spend per period settles at the same adstocked level, so a level can be read as the steady spend per period that holds the channel there.

Both functions describe the response curve the model fitted, which is not the same thing as what would happen if you actually spent that much. The curve is identified only over the range of spend the data contains; asking a saturated Hill curve what happens at ten times the observed maximum returns a number, and that number is extrapolation. spend_for() returns NA rather than a fabricated answer when the target lies beyond max_spend, but it cannot tell you that a reachable target is outside the data's support. Check the range of the adstocked series yourself; plot() shades the levels outside it when given the series as observed.

See also

plot.mm_response_curve(), saturate(), mroi(), and marginal_roi() for the marginal return on raw spend through the full transform

Examples

# The curve mm_weekly's television was simulated with: coefficient 5200,
# half_max 2250 and shape 1.6, on adstocked weekly spend.
data(mm_weekly)
truth <- attr(mm_weekly, "truth")
c(truth$beta[["tv"]], truth$half_max[["tv"]], truth$shape[["tv"]])
#> [1] 5200.0 2250.0    1.6

# A concave curve: marginal return falls from the first pound onward.
concave <- response_curve(
  spend = seq(0, 5000, by = 1000),
  coefficient = 5200, half_max = 2250, shape = 1
)
concave
#>   spend response  marginal
#> 1     0    0.000 2.3111041
#> 2  1000 1600.000 1.1076949
#> 3  2000 2447.059 0.6477545
#> 4  3000 2971.429 0.4244933
#> 5  4000 3328.000 0.2995231
#> 6  5000 3586.207 0.2225948
all(diff(concave$marginal) < 0)
#> [1] TRUE

# An S-curve: marginal return rises up to the curve's steepest point, near
# 900 here, and falls after it. Below that point each extra pound returns
# more than the one before, so the curve is not yet saturated there; whether
# the channel deserves more budget depends on how its marginal return
# compares with other channels' and with break-even.
s_curve <- response_curve(
  spend = seq(0, 5000, by = 500),
  coefficient = 5200, half_max = 2250, shape = 1.6
)
s_curve
#>    spend  response    marginal
#> 1      0    0.0000 0.001128472
#> 2    500  429.9182 1.261993634
#> 3   1000 1115.8577 1.402248359
#> 4   1500 1785.0175 1.250419105
#> 5   2000 2355.7338 1.030821918
#> 6   2500 2818.6324 0.826120871
#> 7   3000 3188.0331 0.657873910
#> 8   3500 3482.5595 0.525816116
#> 9   4000 3718.8362 0.423714294
#> 10  4500 3910.1361 0.344863577
#> 11  5000 4066.6239 0.283637139
s_curve$spend[which.max(s_curve$marginal)]
#> [1] 1000

# What adstocked spend achieves a response of 2000?
spend_for(target = 2000, coefficient = 5200, half_max = 2250, shape = 1.6)
#> [1] 1677.288

# An unbounded curve needs an explicit search range
spend_for(target = 200000, coefficient = 5200, type = "power",
          exponent = 0.5, max_spend = 1e6)
#> [1] 1479.29
